params.place: a lit studio stage: the first Motorola handset on sale standing tall beside a modern phone

moments.what: the old handset, labelled Motorola from the first frame, turns on its plinth as its wordmark plate lights
its antenna catches the rim light
the modern phone beside it lights up and hops, tiny against it, as the camera pushes in
a clay brick slides in next to it, the same block shape, and a label writes on: brick
close on the handset's keypad, its buttons lighting one by one

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Motorola's first phone you could carry was a brick. Why?

params.place: an engineering workbench from the seventies at night, a wall calendar above it

moments.what: soldering irons glow and circuit boards slide across the bench
the wall calendar's pages start tearing off one after another
the weeks figure slams onto the calendar in amber
parts of the handset snap together on the bench
pull back: a briefcase and a meeting badge beside the finished prototype
a label writes on over the badge: the regulators' meeting

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Its engineers had just 6 weeks to build one, to show America's phone regulators.

params.place: above the workbench: the prototype opened up, its parts floating apart in a column of light

moments.what: the handset's shell lifts away
the parts hover in a stack above the bench
a hand outline traces round the handset's grip
the radio boards slide out and glow green, a label writes on
the antenna rises out of the top and lights, labelled
the battery pack drops out of the bottom, the heaviest block, labelled
power lines light from the battery up into the boards

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Everything had to fit in one hand: a radio, an antenna, and a battery to power them.

params.place: a city block at night from above, the handset on a street corner and a radio tower on a rooftop

moments.what: close on the handset's mouthpiece, a phone cord that isn't there fades and snaps away
the handset's red display blinks
a cut wire falls away
the radio board inside glows through the shell
the keypad lights up
a sound wave pulses out of the mouthpiece
rings of radio waves spread out over the street
the camera rises to the rooftop tower as the waves reach it and it lights
the tower's dish blinks back

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: How does it call with no wire? The radio turns your voice into radio waves for a tower nearby.

params.place: high above the city: the towers' patches drawn as a honeycomb of glowing hexagons

moments.what: towers light one after another across the city
a glowing hexagon spreads out round each tower
one hexagon lifts and glows amber
a label writes on in the hexagon: cell
a dot for the handset crosses from one hexagon into the next and the call follows it
the camera dives down onto the handset at the centre

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Each tower covers one small patch, a cell. That's the cell in cell phone.

params.place: a New York street in daylight, tall buildings and a crossing, the prototype raised to someone's ear

moments.what: a street banner with the date lands over the crossing as the camera glides down the avenue
the camera sweeps on down the avenue toward the crossing
a passer-by walks up the far pavement
a figure on the pavement lifts the prototype to his ear
a signal arc leaps from the handset to a rooftop tower
close on the handset as its light blinks with the call
the passer-by turns to look
the handset's display blinks again over the street

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: In April of 1973 it made a real call, on a New York street.

params.place: a shop counter: the first handset on sale on a weighing scale, a modern phone beside it at true size

moments.what: the prototype stands on a shop counter as the shutter behind it rolls down
a NOT FOR SALE label writes on beside it
the shutter starts rolling up on the shop's shelves
the shop is open: the first handset on sale stands over the scale
the handset drops onto a weighing scale and the needle swings
the scale's display counts up to the weight
a modern phone slides in beside it on the counter
a length bracket runs up the old handset
the camera pulls back to show both standing side by side

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: But that phone wasn't for sale. The first one you could buy weighed 785 grams, and was 300 millimetres long.

params.place: a long glowing timeline rail in the dark, prototype handsets standing along it from the street call to the shop

moments.what: the camera starts flying along the rail past prototype handsets
each prototype is a little smaller and neater than the last
the camera turns toward the far end of the rail
the shop at the far end of the rail lights its window
the rail lights up end to end
the money figure lands on the shop's sign board in amber
the MOTOROLA wordmark glows over the rail
the rail pulses from end to end
the camera settles on the shop front
the years figure counts up on the shop's lit window
the prototypes light one by one along the rail

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Getting that brick into a shop took over $100M of Motorola's money, and more than 10 years.

params.place: back on the lit studio stage, the handset on its plinth beside the modern phone

moments.what: the rail's light flows into the handset's keypad
the handset turns on its plinth
the camera pulls back past the modern phone, its screen glowing
a hand outline traces round the grip
the wide stage shot of the first frame, the antenna catching the rim light

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: All of that, for a phone that fit in one hand.

disclaimer: Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.
sources: Data: Motorola Solutions · Guinness World Records · Sep 1983
